original_text:
You don't need to know all of SQL.
You just need to know the 20% you'll use every day.
👇

When I first started learning SQL, I tried to memorize everything.
Every function.
Every clause.
Every keyword.
The problem?
I rarely used most of them.

Over time, I realized the same patterns kept showing up.
• Filtering and aggregating data
• Joining tables
• Window functions
• CTEs
• CASE WHEN logic
• Working with dates
• Sorting results

If you get comfortable with these concepts, you'll solve the majority of SQL problems you'll see at work and in interviews.

The rest?

You'll learn naturally as new problems come up.

That's one of the reasons SQL has stayed relevant for decades.

It's not about memorizing syntax.

It's about knowing which pattern to reach for.

💾 Save this cheat sheet for your next SQL interview.

💬 If you could only master one SQL topic, which one would it be?

Follow for more simple breakdowns on SQL, data engineering, and Gen AI.

ai_analysis.summary: This short, high-level SQL post argues that learners should master recurring problem-solving patterns rather than memorize every function, clause, or keyword. It lists filtering and aggregation, joining tables, window functions, CTEs, CASE WHEN logic, working with dates, and sorting results, claiming that familiarity with these patterns covers most SQL problems encountered at work and in interviews. It does not explain syntax, provide examples, or identify the exact subset referred to as the "20%" used every day.

interview_questions.question: Which recurring SQL patterns does the post prioritize for everyday work and interviews?
interview_questions.answer:
The post identifies filtering and aggregating data as a recurring pattern.
It also lists joining tables, window functions, and CTEs.
Conditional logic with CASE WHEN, working with dates, and sorting results are additional priorities.

interview_questions.question: Why does the author recommend mastering SQL patterns instead of memorizing every SQL feature?
interview_questions.answer:
The author found that most functions, clauses, and keywords were rarely used while solving practical problems.
Recurring patterns appeared frequently and were presented as sufficient for most everyday and interview problems.
Additional SQL knowledge can be learned naturally as new problems arise.

interview_questions.question: According to the post, how should a learner approach an unfamiliar SQL problem?
interview_questions.answer:
The learner should identify the recurring SQL pattern that matches the problem rather than trying to recall every available feature.
If the solution requires knowledge beyond the familiar patterns, the learner can learn that capability when the new problem presents it.
